prize_parts.citation: For a body of work that renews lyric, verse narrative and the essay through classical learning, translation and elegy, and that gives hybrid form emotional and intellectual weight.

statement.case_for: Carson has an unmistakable voice and a formal inventiveness that serves her subject rather than decorating it. In Autobiography of Red, the Geryon myth becomes a modern verse novel. In Nox, an elegy for her brother is built from a Catullus translation, archive and fragment. Her scholarship, translations and essays feed her poetry, so philological rigor and lyric risk are not separate activities. She has published over several decades and kept finding new forms, so the case does not rest on one landmark book. I come to this as a writer of non-fiction who works from archives, and I am drawn to a poet whose research becomes literary form. My own practice is context only and does not establish merit. The achievement lies in the joining of antiquity, grief and desire, and it looks durable. Within Nobel's will, I read the 'ideal direction' as a matter of depth and seriousness of imaginative purpose, and I think that is met here.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that much of Carson's effect depends on page layout, typography, the book as object and the relation to ancient Greek texts. A committee reading in translation, or from ordinary editions, may see only part of it. Her corpus is also smaller and more fragmentary than a novelist's, and a good deal of it consists of translation and adaptation. It is a fair question whether the hybrid, scholarly mode is sustained depth or sometimes erudite play, and whether it reaches the broad significance across a whole oeuvre that the prize implies. These are real doubts and I have not resolved them.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Cărtărescu first for visionary, encyclopedic prose of high imaginative depth. He also asks how much of Carson's oeuvre is original creation as opposed to translation and adaptation, and whether her formal play is sometimes mannered.
responses.response: The authorship question is fair and bears on whether the citation scope holds. I would answer that in her strongest books the translation and the original verse are not separable. Nox is built around a translation but is plainly her own elegy, and Autobiography of Red reworks Stesichorus into new narrative. That argues for a citation that names the hybrid method rather than the translations as such. The mannerism risk is real, and I cannot fully discount it. I do not accept that Cărtărescu's claim is stronger on sustained quality, because you note it rests on a few very large works and that the late novels may be uneven. Both writers carry a corpus risk, and I find Carson's formal development across books more convincing than long-form repetition. I keep Cărtărescu as my first alternative and do not treat the gap as large.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first for a recognisable metaphysical world of memory and the body. She places Carson second and observes that Nox is a material object, so the achievement does not reduce to text on a page. She also doubts whether translation and adaptation belong to the core literary achievement.
responses.response: I share the concern about the book-object. It is the main reason I would not call this case settled. My view is that the writing in Nox, the fragments, the translation notes and the elegiac voice, carries real literary weight without the physical form. The folded object adds to the work and is not what the case rests on. On translation, I would not treat it as peripheral for Carson, since her engagement with Greek sources runs through the whole body of work and shapes her poetry. I accept your point that Cărtărescu's voice is very distinctive. Where we differ is on how much weight to give a single cosmology realized at novel scale compared with continual formal renewal. Neither of us can judge Romanian sentence-level texture, and your own uncertainty on that point is one I share.

responses.point: Sward ranks Carson first as a distinctive voice whose hybrid work carries emotional and intellectual weight. She asks whether the hybrid form counts as idealistic literature in the sense of Nobel's will or is more a scholarly-poetic achievement.
responses.response: I agree that this is the question the committee has to answer openly, and I would not wave it away. My reading is that 'idealistic' need not exclude learning. The ideal direction is shown by seriousness of purpose and depth, and in Nox that purpose is grief rendered through the act of translating, which is not merely scholarly. I would add a caution to your support: the case depends on how we read the will, and I do not want agreement on Carson to cover over that difference. If a colleague reads the will more narrowly, Adonis, whom you place fourth, offers a different kind of ideal significance in the remaking of a poetic language. I would want that argued on literary grounds and not on reputation.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Carson first and adds Sappho and Antigonick as public-knowledge examples of her classical reworkings. He calls the hybrid corpus partly a matter of interpretation for 'sustained quality', and he doubts whether her latest output matches the 1998-2010 peak.
responses.response: Your point about the later output is the most useful qualification, and I can neither confirm nor dispel it from public knowledge. If the peak lies in roughly 1998-2010, the citation should be drawn from the established core and should not claim that the recent work equals it. I would keep the wording to the renewal of verse narrative, elegy and the essay, and leave the later books out of the claim. On interpretation of 'sustained quality', I would say the test is whether she keeps finding new forms rather than whether every book matches the best. Her record seems to meet that test, but it is a judgment and I do not hold it as established.

uncertainties: I have not independently verified any text, and my assessment rests on general public knowledge of the major works.
How far the book-object and typographic dimensions of Carson's work survive in translation and ordinary editions is unresolved.
Whether her recent output sustains the level of the best-known books is unverified.
How the committee reads the 'ideal direction' in Nobel's will, and whether a hybrid scholarly-poetic mode fits it, is unsettled.
The tension between concentrated, formally radical work and bulk across the oeuvre is not resolved, and it also affects the Cărtărescu and Michon comparisons.
Translation loss for Romanian, Arabic and French prosody and syntax limits any comparison with B028, B044 and B015.
Carlberg's committee voting status is undocumented, so her simulated vote is a modeling assumption and should not be read as a record of actual influence.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. The profile records no personal, professional or family connection to Anne Carson, Mircea Cărtărescu or Adonis. Her institutional connections are limited to Swedish Academy colleagues, including Steve Sem-Sandberg, who was elected alongside her in 2020.
